newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leader under pressure as exodus grows.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leader under pressure as exodus grows.

text.p: U.S. military helicopters airlifted Americans and other foreigners from Tirana on Saturday while hundreds of Albanians fled to Italy in a makeshift flotilla of rusty merchant ships and fishing boats and European governments agonised over whether they should intervene.

Although Tirana was calmer after a show of force by police, thousands of Albanians broke through police lines in the port of Durres in a desperate attempt to board a Greek frigate that had come to evacuate foreign diplomats.

After weeks of anarchy following the collapse of shady investment schemes in which thousands of Albanians lost their savings, President Sali Berisha came under international pressure to quit, a key demand of rebels in the south.

Italy, Albania's biggest economic partner and a leading player in international efforts to halt the country's slide into chaos, signalled that Berisha was no longer a key player and his fate was in the hands of Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told the newspaper La Repubblica that Fino had to decide whether Berisha's presence was "an obstacle to pacifying the country or not, whether his continuation in the role can be accepted at least to prepare elections or not".
In the Dutch town of Apeldoorn, where EU foreign ministers were discussing the crisis, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said openly that Berisha should resign.

"I'm sure that if President Berisha were to step down that would in some ways improve the situation in Albania," said Petersen, whose country holds the chairmanship of the 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Italy said it would give temporary sanctuary to fleeing Albanians but intended to repatriate them once the armed anarchy in their country had subsided.

A senior government official, Nicola Sinisi, announced the policy after a two-hour meeting of police and immigration chiefs held in response to a recent influx of some 1,600 Albanians in a convoy of creaking boats.
Italian Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said the country should brace for a mass influx of refugees.
An Albanian military helicopter landed in southern Italy with 33 refugees on board, including five children.

The exodus has raised fears in Italy of a repeat of the tide of 40,000 Albanians who flooded into southeast ports and sparked serious rioting in 1991 after Stalinist rule crumbled in Europe's poorest state.

In Durres, where diplomats and foreign nationals have been evacuated over the past few days, police fired in the air to try and hold back a crowd of 5,000 Albanians desperate to board a Greek warship.
But after running two km (one mile) through the port, they reached the keyside just in time to see the ship steaming away.
The U.S. evacuation, suspended on Friday after two Marine Cobra helicopters were fired on, restarted at dawn on Saturday and by midday more than 120 people had been brought out.

Tirana was quieter on Saturday, with the level of gunfire greatly reduced. Authorities facing a nationwide slide into anarchy have sought to restore order by parading armoured vehicles on the streets and raising police pay.
Justice Minister Spartak Ngjela said the government had set up special, highly paid, police units to disarm gunmen who have brought the country to anarchy.
The move is clearly aimed at tackling the lawlessness ripping the country apart after civilians looted barracks as the army disintegrated and nervous police melted away.
At one of Tirana's main police stations, about 200 men were waiting outside to join the new units. Uniformed police were on the streets again after having disappeared several days ago.
Albanian state television showed pictures of what it said were weapons surrendered in Tirana. But in the south, rebel leaders said they would not hand in their guns until Berisha resigned.

The United States has so far evacuated more than 600 people from Tirana, which in recent days has been the scene of growing lawlessness with people looting rifles from arms depots and loosing off bursts of gunfire into the air.
In Vienna, OSCE ambassadors agreed to give broad support to sending foreign troops to Albania.
The 54-nation group backed a proposal by its mediator in Albania, Franz Vranitzky, to ask foreign governments to send forces, but no state gave a commitment to do so.
In Apeldoorn, EU foreign ministers were divided on Saturday on whether to back calls for military intervention.
Sweden's Lena Hjelm-Wallen was blunt about the EU's predicament. "Frankly, we don't know what to do," she told reporters.
